Do you not see them saying "qad qamati al-salah" (the prayer has been established), before the moment of its establishment? So the meaning of the verse is: success has already been attained by them, and they are in it now.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿIkrimah, ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited (qad uflih) with a damma on the alif, a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ha, in the passive form (ʿala ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: the believers have obtained lasting endurance in good. As for the one who recites (qad uflih) with a damma on the alif, its meaning is: they have been brought to success.

The root meaning of *khushuʿ* (humble submission) in the language is submission and humility.

Concerning what is meant by *khushuʿ* in prayer, there are four opinions:

The first: it is looking at the place of prostration. Abu Hurairah reported: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-460) prayed, he would raise his gaze to the sky, then the verse ﴿those who are humble in their prayer﴾ was revealed, and he lowered his head." Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah held this view.

The second: it is refraining from turning one's attention during prayer, and lowering one's wing (kanaf) to the Muslim man. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said this.

The third: it is stillness during prayer. Mujahid, Ibrahim and al-Zuhri said this.

The fourth: it is fear. al-Hasan said this.

Concerning what is meant by *laghw* (idle, vain talk) here, there are five opinions:

The first: it is polytheism. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is falsehood. Ibn Abi Talhah narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: it is sins. al-Hasan said this. The fourth: it is lying. al-Suddi said this. The fifth: it is the insults and harm that they heard from the disbelievers. Muqatil said this. Al-Zajjaj said: *Laghw* is every play and amusement, and every act of disobedience is cast aside and discarded. So the meaning is: earnestness in what Allah commanded them occupied them away from idle talk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and who are active in giving zakah﴾ means: those who pay it. He expressed paying it with the verb "doing" because they did it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except from their wives﴾. Al-Farraʾ said: "ʿala" here has the meaning of "min" (from). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that they are blamed for indulging in what was forbidden to them and what they were commanded to guard, except with regard to their wives or what their right hands possess; for they are not blamed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that﴾ means: whoever seeks (ibtagha), (p-461) i.e., desires, beyond that, namely beyond wives and those owned; ﴿those are the transgressors﴾ means: the oppressors and wrongdoers, because they have overstepped to what is not lawful.

His saying: ﴿and who are, for their trusts and their covenant, attentive﴾. Ibn Kathir recited (li-amanatihim) in the singular, which is a collective noun. The meaning is: for the trusts that they were entrusted with. Sometimes the trust is between the servant and his Lord, and sometimes it is between him and his fellow human beings, so it is incumbent upon him to observe all of them; likewise the covenant. The meaning of (ra'un) is: keepers, guardians. Al-Zajjaj said: The root meaning of *ra'y* (shepherding, guarding) in the language is standing over the upkeep of whatever the shepherd is responsible for, of everything.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿upon their prayers﴾. Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir recited (salawatihim) in the plural. Hamzah and al-Kisai recited (salatihim) in the singular, as a collective noun. Guarding the prayers (al-muhafazah) means performing them at their appointed times.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿those are the inheritors﴾. al-Suddi reported from his shaykhs that Allah, the Exalted, raises Paradise for the disbelievers so that they look at their homes in it, had they obeyed; then it is divided among the believers, and they inherit them. That is His saying: ﴿those are the inheritors﴾. We have explained this in (al-Aʿraf: 43) at His saying: ﴿you have been given it as an inheritance﴾, and we have explained the meaning of *al-Firdaws* in (al-Kahf: 107).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 12–16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We created man﴾ — there are two opinions concerning it.

One: that it refers to Adam, peace be upon him. It is said ﴿from an extract of clay﴾ because he was extracted (istulla) from all of the earth. This is the view of Salman al-Farisi, Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, and Qatadah.

The second: that it refers to the son of Adam, and the sulalah (extract) is the sperm-drop extracted from the clay, and the clay is Adam, peace be upon him. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: sulalah is on the pattern fu'alah, and it denotes what is extracted in small amounts. Every noun built on the pattern fu'alah is meant to indicate a small quantity, such as fudalah (leftover), nukhalah (bran), and qulamah (paring).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We made him﴾ — meaning the son of Adam — ﴿a drop of sperm in a firm place﴾, which is the womb, ﴿secure﴾; that is, protected, having been prepared for his settling in it. We have explained the meanings of nutfah, 'alaqah, and mudghah in Surah al-Hajj (22:5).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We made the lump into bones﴾ — Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ('izaman, fakasawna al-izama) in the plural. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ('azman, fakasawna al-'azma) in the singular.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ — this is the seventh stage. 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: "She is not a buried infant (mawudah) until she passes through the seven stages."

Concerning the locus of this production there are two opinions:

One: that it is the mother's womb. Then, concerning the manner of this production, there are two opinions: one, that it is the breathing of the spirit into him, related by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and others. The second: that He made him male or female, said by al-Hasan.

The second opinion: that it is after his coming out from his mother's womb. Then, concerning the manner of this production, there are four opinions: First, that the beginning of that production was that he cried out (istahalla), then he was guided to the breast, and he learned how to stretch his legs until he sat, until he stood on his feet, until he walked, until he was weaned, until he reached puberty, until he moved about in the lands; related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is the maturity of youth, said by Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid. The third: that it is the emergence of teeth and hair, said by al-Dahhak; it was said to him: "Is he not born with hair on his head?" He replied: "Then where are the pubic and armpit hair?" The fourth: that it is the granting of intellect and understanding, related by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾ — that is, He deserves glorification and praise. We have explained the meaning of "tabaraka" in Surah al-A'raf (7:54). ﴿the best of creators﴾ — that is, the best of those who form and determine. Khalq in the language means determination (taqdir). It has come in a hadith that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse while 'Umar was present, up to His saying ﴿another creation﴾, and 'Umar said: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You have been answered with what you have said, O son of al-Khattab.'"

If it is asked: how is His saying ﴿the best of creators﴾ reconciled with His saying ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah?﴾ (35:3)?

The answer: khalq can mean bringing into existence (ijad), and there is no originator other than Allah; and it can mean determination (taqdir), as in the saying of Zuhair:

"And you indeed measure what you have determined, but some people determine and do not measure."

This is what is meant here: that the children of Adam may form, determine, and make things, so Allah is the best of formers and determiners. Al-Akhfash said: "The creators here are the craftsmen, so Allah is the best of creators."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed you, after that﴾ — that is, after what has been mentioned of the completion of creation — ﴿will surely die﴾ at the end of your terms. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (la-ma'tuna) with an alif. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say of one who has not died: "You are going to die (ma'it) in a little while," and "dead (mayyit)." They do not say of one who has already died, "This is dying (ma'it)"; it is said only of the future. Likewise it is said: "This is the chief of his people today," and when you inform that he will lead them in a little while, you say: "This is about to lead his people in a little while (sa'id)." Likewise: "This is the noble of the people," and "This is about to be (sharif)." This whole pattern in Arabic is as I have described to you.

The third: that it is the emergence of teeth and hair, said by al-Dahhak; it was said to him: "Is he not born with hair on his head?" He replied: "Then where are the pubic and armpit hair?" The fourth: that it is the granting of intellect and understanding, related by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾ — that is, He deserves glorification and praise. We have explained the meaning of "tabaraka" in Surah al-A'raf (7:54). ﴿the best of creators﴾ — that is, the best of those who form and determine. Khalq in the language means determination (taqdir). It has come in a hadith that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse while 'Umar was present, up to His saying ﴿another creation﴾, and 'Umar said: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You have been answered with what you have said, O son of al-Khattab.'"

If it is asked: how is His saying ﴿the best of creators﴾ reconciled with His saying ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah?﴾ (35:3)?

The answer: khalq can mean bringing into existence (ijad), and there is no originator other than Allah; and it can mean determination (taqdir), as in the saying of Zuhair:

"And you indeed measure what you have determined, but some people determine and do not measure."

This is what is meant here: that the children of Adam may form, determine, and make things, so Allah is the best of formers and determiners. Al-Akhfash said: "The creators here are the craftsmen, so Allah is the best of creators."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed you, after that﴾ — that is, after what has been mentioned of the completion of creation — ﴿will surely die﴾ at the end of your terms. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (la-ma'tuna) with an alif. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say of one who has not died: "You are going to die (ma'it) in a little while," and "dead (mayyit)." They do not say of one who has already died, "This is dying (ma'it)"; it is said only of the future. Likewise it is said: "This is the chief of his people today," and when you inform that he will lead them in a little while, you say: "This is about to lead his people in a little while (sa'id)." Likewise: "This is the noble of the people," and "This is about to be (sharif)." This whole pattern in Arabic is as I have described to you.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 23, verses 17–20**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths﴾. He means: the seven heavens. Al-Zajjaj (grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: each one is a *tariqa* (path). Ibn Qutayba (scholar of language and hadith) said: they were called *tara'iq* (paths) from *tatāruq* (layering), because some of them are above others. It is said: *tāraqtu al-shay'* ("I layered the thing") when you place some of it above others.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We were not unaware of creation﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: We were not heedless of them when We built above them a sky in which We set the sun, the moon and the stars.

Second: We would not leave them without provision, so We sent down the rain.

Third: We did not neglect guarding them from the sky falling upon them and destroying them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure﴾, which Allah knows. Muqatil (Muqatil ibn Sulayman, Qur'an commentator) said: in the measure that suffices them for their livelihood.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a tree﴾. It is conjoined to His saying ﴿gardens﴾. Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Ya'mur and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i (Qur'an readers) read *wa-shajaratun* (وَشَجَرَةٌ) with a *ḍamma* (raised case). The tree intended here is the olive tree.

If it is asked: why did He single out this tree from among trees?

The answer is in four aspects:

First: because of how greatly they benefit from it. He reminded them of the blessings they know. Likewise, in the first verse He singled out the date palms and the grapevines, because these were the main fruits of the Hijaz and its environs; the date palms belonged to the people of Madina, and the grapevines to the people of al-Ta'if.

Second: because they hardly ever tend it with watering, and it produces the fruit from which oil is obtained.

Third: because it grows with water, which is the opposite of fire, and in its fruit there is life for fire and fuel for it.

Fourth: because the first olive tree that grew in that place, according to what Muqatil claimed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Tūri Sīnā'﴾ (Mount Sinai). Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *Ṭūri Sīnīn* (طُورِ سِينِينَ) with a *kasra* on the *sīn*. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, and all of them read it with a long vowel (*madd*). Al-Farra' (grammarian) said: the Arabs say *Sīnā'* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn* in all dialects, except the Banu Kinana, who use a *kasra* on the *sīn*. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi, grammarian) said: this word is not declined (*lā tanṣarif*), because it was made the name of a region or land; likewise *Sīnīn*. If it had been made the name of a place, or of a dwelling, or something similar among masculine nouns, it would have been declined, because you would have named a masculine thing with a masculine name. *Ṭūr* means: mountain.

Regarding the meaning of *Sīnā'* there are five opinions:

First: that it means "the beautiful," narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak said: *al-Ṭūr* is "the mountain" in Syriac, and *Sīnā'* is "the beautiful" in Nabataean. 'Ata' said: he means the beautiful mountain.

Second: that it means "the blessed," narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: that it is the name of a particular kind of stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it is found there. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: that *Ṭūr Sīnā'* is the mountain covered with trees. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fifth: that *Sīnā'* is the name of the place where this mountain is. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi (commentator) said: this is the most correct of the opinions. Ibn Zayd said: this is the mountain from which Musa was called, and it lies between Egypt and Aqaba.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿grows with oil﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *tunbitu* (تُنْبِتُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *kasra* on the *bā'*. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *tanbutu* (تَنْبُتُ) with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *bā'*. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, *nabatat* and *anbatat*. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: it is said that *nabata al-shajaru* and *anbata al-shajaru* have the same meaning. Zuhayr said:

*You saw people in need around their dwellings, a settled company for them, until the herbage sprouted.*

He (al-Zajjaj) said: the meaning of ﴿tanbutu bi-l-duhn﴾ is: it grows along with oil, just as you say: "Zayd came to me with the sword," meaning: he came to me and the sword was with him. Abu 'Ubayda (grammarian) said: the meaning of the verse is: it grows oil, and the *bā'* is extra (*zā'ida*), as in His saying: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. We have explained this meaning there.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and condiment﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read *wa-ṣibghan* (وَصِبْغًا) with a *fatḥa*. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *wa-ṣibāghin* (وَصِبَاغٍ) with a long *alif* and a *kasra*. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ṣibgh* is like *al-ṣibāgh*, just as it is said *dibgh* and *dibāgh*, and *libs* and *libās*. The exegetes said: what is meant by *al-ṣibgh* here is olive oil, because it colours the bread when it is dipped in it; the meaning is that it is a condiment in which bread is dipped.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verse 23–44:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾. The exegetes said: This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by mentioning this patient Messenger, so that he might take him as an example in his patience, and so that he would know that the messengers before him had also been denied.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He wants to make himself superior over you﴾; that is, to exalt himself over you with superiority, so that he becomes one who is followed. ﴿And if Allah had willed﴾ that nothing be worshipped besides Him, ﴿He would have sent down angels﴾ to convey His command; He did not send a human being. ﴿We have not heard of this﴾ which Noah calls us to of monotheism ﴿among our forefathers of old﴾. As for "al-Jinnah" (madness), its meaning is insanity.

Regarding His words ﴿until a time﴾ there are two opinions:

One of them: it is death, so its meaning is: wait for his death. The second: it is an unspecified time.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me"﴾. Ikrimah and Ibn Muhaysin read: (Qala Rabbu) with a damma on the ba', and in the other account [al-Mu'minun: 39].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿for that they have denied me﴾. Ya'qub read: (kadhdhabuni) with a yaa' (the first-person suffix), and in the account that follows it also: (fattaquni) [al-Mu'minun: 52], (an yahdurun) [al-Mu'minun: 98], (Rabbi irji'uni) [al-Mu'minun: 99], (wa la tukallimun) [al-Mu'minun: 108]; Ya'qub affirmed them in both states. The meaning: help me by their denial; that is, help me by destroying them as a recompense for them for their denial. ﴿So We revealed to him﴾ — we have explained it in (Hud: 37) up to His words ﴿then embark therein﴾; that is, enter into your ship. ﴿Of every kind, two of each pair﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: (min kulli) with a kasra on the lam without tanwin. Hafs from 'Asim read: (min kullin) with tanwin. Abu 'Ali said: The reading of the majority is the idafa of "kull" to "zawjayn" (two spouses), and the reading of Hafs returns to "zawjayn," because the meaning is: from every one of the pairs, two.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read: (munzalan) with a damma on the mim. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim its fatha. The manzil (with a fatha on the mim) is the name for every place where you alight, and the manzil (with a damma) is the verbal noun meaning the act of causing to descend; it is said: I caused him to descend (anzaltuhu inzalan) and manzilan.

Regarding the time when Noah said that, there are two opinions:

One of them: when he entered the ship. The second: when he disembarked from the ship.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs; and indeed We were ever testing﴾; that is, indeed We were ever testing them by sending Noah to them. ﴿Then We produced after them another generation﴾ meaning: 'Ad, ﴿and sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾, who was Hud; this is the saying of most of them. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: they were Thamud and the messenger was Salih. What follows is clear up to His words ﴿Does he promise you that you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "annakum" is in the accusative, meaning: "Does he promise you [that you] will be brought out when you die?" Since the speech was long, the mention of "anna" was repeated, as in His words: ﴿Did they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawbah: 63].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Far, far is that which you are promised﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (hayhata hayhata) with a fatha on the ta' in both in connected speech and with sukun in pause. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz and Harun from Abu 'Amr read: (hayhatan hayhatan) with the accusative and tanwin. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Asim al-Jahdari, Abu Hayawa al-Hadrami and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: (hayhatun hayhatun) with the nominative and tanwin. Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah read: (hayhatin hayhatin) with the genitive and tanwin. Abu Ja'far read: (hayhati hayhati) with the genitive without tanwin, and he would pause with the ha'. Abu al-Mutawakkil, al-Nahiji, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah read: (hayhatu hayhatu) with the nominative without tanwin. Mu'adh al-Qari', Ibn Ya'mur, Abu Raja' and Kharijah from Abu 'Amr read: (hayhat hayhat) with sukun on the ta' in both. "Hayhata" has ten dialectal forms, of which we have mentioned seven from the readers; the eighth is (ayhata), the ninth is (ayhana) with a nun, and the tenth is (ayha) without a nun; Ibn al-Qasim mentioned them. Al-Ahwas recited, combining two of these dialects:

Remember days that passed from youth, and far, far from you is their return.

Al-Zajjaj said: As for the fatha, pausing on it is with the ha', you say: (hayhah) if you open and pause after the fatha; if you kasra and pause on the ta', you are one who uses tanwin in connected speech, or one who does not use tanwin. The interpretation of "hayhata" is: distance from what you are promised. When you say: (hayhata ma qulta), its meaning is: far is what you said. When you say: (hayhata lima qulta), its meaning is: distance for what you said. It is said: (ayhata) has the meaning of (hayhata), and they recited:

And ayhat, ayhat is al-'Aqiq and whoever is in it, and ayhat is union with al-'Aqiq, which we seek.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: If you pause on "hayhata," say: "hayhah." Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i prefers pausing with the ha', and I prefer the ta'.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿for what you are promised﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: (ma tu'adun) without the lam. The exegetes said: The people deemed unlikely their being resurrected after death, heedless of reflecting on the beginning of their creation and Allah's power to originate them; and by this deeming unlikely they meant that it would never happen. ﴿It is only our life of this world﴾; they mean: life is nothing but what we are in, and there is no life after death.

If it is asked: how did they say ﴿We die and live﴾ when they did not acknowledge resurrection?

Al-Zajjaj mentioned three answers regarding this:

One: we die and our children live, so it is as if they said: a people die and a people live.

The second: we live and then die, because the waw denotes conjunction, not sequence.

The third: our beginning is dead in the origin of creation, then we live, then we die.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He is not but﴾; they mean the Messenger. The explanation of what follows this has already passed [Hud: 7; al-Nahl: 38] up to His words ﴿He said, "After a little while"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "after a little while," and "ma" is superfluous, meaning emphasis.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will surely become regretful﴾; that is, over their disbelief. ﴿So the shout seized them in truth﴾; that is, by their deserving the punishment for their disbelief. The exegetes said: Jibril shouted at them a cry by which the earth shook beneath them, so they became, because of its intensity, like debris. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-ghuthaʾ is what resembles foam, and what rises upon the flood, and the like of that which is of no benefit at all. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: We made them destroyed like the ghuthaʾ, which is what the flood carries up of foam and refuse, for it goes away and scatters. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ghuthaʾ is the perished and withered leaves of trees which, when the flood runs, you see mixed with its foam. The explanation of what follows has already been given [al-Hijr: 5] up to His words, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read: (tatra kulla ma) with tanwin, and the pause is with an alif. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read without tanwin, and pausing according to Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir is with an alif. Hubayrah and Hafs narrated from 'Asim that he pauses with a yaa'. Abu 'Ali said: by his saying "pauses with a yaa'," he means: with an inclined alif. Al-Farra' said: most of the Arabs omit tanwin, and some use tanwin. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: We follow up with an interval between each two messengers, and it is from "tawatur" (succession), and the origin is "wutra," then the waw was changed to ta', as they changed it in "taqwa" and "tukhmah." Al-Zajjaj related from al-Asma'i that he said: the meaning of "watartu al-khabar" is: I made one part of it follow another, with a short pause between the two reports. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: Among what the common people place in the wrong position is their saying: "My letters have come to you in succession (tawatarat)," meaning: they connected without interruption; so they put tawatur in the place of ittisal (continuity), and that is an error. Tawatur is only the coming of a thing, then its cessation, then its coming again, and it is the tafa'ul form from witr (odd, single); it is said: "watartu al-khabar": I made one part of it follow another, with a short pause between the two reports. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾; its origin is "wutra" from mutawatarah, then the ta' was substituted for the waw, and its meaning is: discontinuous and spaced out, because between every two prophets there was a long age. Abu Hurayrah said: there is no harm in making up Ramadan fasts "tatra," that is, discontinuously. When it is said: "Fulan watara his books," the meaning is: he followed them, and there was an interval between every two books.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We made them follow one another﴾; that is, We destroyed the nations, some after others, ﴿and We made them into tales﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: that is, they are used as an example in evil, and one does not say of good: "I made him a hadith."

Regarding the time when Noah said that, there are two opinions:

One of them: when he entered the ship. The second: when he disembarked from the ship.

Remember days that passed from youth, and far, far from you is their return.

Al-Zajjaj said: As for the fatha, pausing on it is with the ha', you say: (hayhah) if you open and pause after the fatha; if you kasra and pause on the ta', you are one who uses tanwin in connected speech, or one who does not use tanwin. And ayhat, ayhat is al-'Aqiq and whoever is in it, and ayhat is union with al-'Aqiq, which we seek.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: If you pause on "hayhata," say: "hayhah." Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i prefers pausing with the ha', and I prefer the ta'.

The exegetes said: The people deemed unlikely their being resurrected after death, heedless of reflecting on the beginning of their creation and Allah's power to originate them; and by this deeming unlikely they meant that it would never happen. ﴿It is only our life of this world﴾; they mean: life is nothing but what we are in, and there is no life after death.

Al-Zajjaj mentioned three answers regarding this:

One: we die and our children live, so it is as if they said: a people die and a people live.

The second: we live and then die, because the waw denotes conjunction, not sequence.

The third: our beginning is dead in the origin of creation, then we live, then we die.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 49–50:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture﴾. He means the Torah, which He gave to him all at once after the drowning of Pharaoh. ﴿So that they might be guided﴾: He means the Children of Israel. The meaning is: in order that they might be guided.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Abla read *āyatayn* (two signs) in the dual form. This is like His saying: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign﴾ [al-Anbiya: 91], and its explanation has already passed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sheltered them﴾; that is, We made them take refuge, ﴿on a hill﴾ (*rabwah*). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *rubwah* with a *damma* on the *ra'*. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*. We have already explained the meaning of *rabwah* in al-Baqarah: 265. ﴿Of a secure place﴾; that is, level ground on which its inhabitants settle. The meaning is: having a place of settlement. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, having a stable site. ﴿And a spring﴾, which is water flowing from springs. Ibn Qutaybah said: "*Dhat qarar*" means that one can settle there for habitation, and "*ma'in*" is apparent water. It is said that it is a passive form derived from *ʿayn* (spring), as if its original form were *maʿyun*, just as one says *thawb makhit* (a sewn garment) and *burr makil* (measured wheat). (p-476)

The exegetes differed concerning the location of this described hill, in four opinions:

The first: that it is Damascus. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abdullah ibn Salam and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib also said this.

The second: that it is Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis). This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah also said this, and from al-Hasan there are two opinions like this one.

The third: that it is al-Ramlah in the land of Palestine. Abu Hurayrah said this.

The fourth: that it is Egypt. Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib said this.

As for the reason for which they sought refuge on the hill, Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: Mary fled with her son 'Isa from their king, and then she returned to her people after twelve years. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the king had intended to kill 'Isa. (p-477)

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 62–67:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And with Us is a Book﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). ﴿It speaks with the truth﴾: the deeds of creation have been recorded in it, so it speaks of what they do. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, that is, they will not be deprived of the reward for their deeds.

Then He returned to the disbelievers and said: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. Muqatil said: in heedlessness of faith in the Qur'an. Ibn Jarir said: in blindness to this Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that it refers to the righteous deeds described in His saying, ﴿Those hasten to the good deeds﴾, so the meaning would be: rather, the hearts of these people are in blindness about this. It is also possible that it refers to the Book, so the meaning would be: rather, their hearts are in confusion about the Book that speaks with the truth, while their deeds are recorded in it.

Regarding what is indicated by "this" (hadha), there are three opinions:

First: the Qur'an. Second: the righteous deeds. Third: the Preserved Tablet.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

First: evil deeds short of shirk, narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas.

Second: sinful misdeeds beyond that truth, said by Mujahid. Ibn Jarir said: beyond the deeds of the believers and the people of piety and fear (of God).

Third: deeds other than those by which they were described; they will do them, said by al-Zajjaj.

Fourth: deeds, before the time that God, may He be exalted, has decreed for punishing them when it comes, consisting of acts of disobedience, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are doing them﴾ is a report of what they will do of their wicked deeds, which were written against them; they must necessarily perform them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones﴾, that is, their wealthy ones and their leaders, and the reference is to the Quraysh. Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿with the punishment﴾ there are two opinions:

One: the striking of swords on the Day of Badr, said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak.

The second: the hunger with which they were punished for seven years, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. ﴿They cry out﴾ (yajarun) means: they shout. ﴿Do not cry out today﴾, that is, do not seek relief from the punishment. ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾, that is, you will not be protected from Our punishment. ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿but you turned back on your heels﴾, that is, you retreated and held back from faith in them, ﴿arrogant﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). His saying: ﴿by it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), and it is a kinaya (an indirect reference) to something not mentioned. The meaning is: you are arrogant and boast of the House and the Sanctuary, because of your security within it while the rest of the people fear in their own lands. You say: "We are the people of the Sanctuary, so we fear no one, and we are the people of God's House and its custodians." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and others. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also possible that the pronoun in "by it" refers to the Book, so the meaning would be: its recitation to you produces arrogance in you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Samiran﴾. Abu Ubayda said: its meaning is: you abandon (the truth) while gathering in evening conversation (summaran), and samir is in the sense of sumar, like tifl in the place of atfal, and it derives from samar al-layl (night conversation). Ibn Qutayba said: "samiran" means conversing at night, and al-samar is night talk. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn Muhaysin recited (sumaran) with a damma on the sin, a shadda on the mim, and a fatha on it, as the plural of samir. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited (sumaran) with a damma on the sin, a shadda on the mim, and an alif after it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿tahjurun﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (tahjurun) with a fatha on the ta and a damma on the jim. Regarding its meaning there are four opinions:

First: you abandon the remembrance of God and the truth, narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

Second: you abandon the Book of God and His Prophet (ﷺ), said by al-Hasan.

Third: you abandon the House, said by Abu Salih. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Quraysh used to converse around the House and boast of it, but they did not circumambulate it.

Fourth: you say abusive speech (hujran) of the kind that is idle talk and raving, said by Ibn Qutayba. Al-Farra' said: it is said that a man "has hajara in his sleep" when he raves. The meaning is: you say about the Messenger of God (ﷺ) what is not in him and what does not harm him.

Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin, and Nafi' recited (tuhjarun) with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the jim. Ibn Qutayba said: this is from al-hajr, which is reviling and vulgar speech, meaning their reviling of the Prophet (ﷺ) and those who followed him. Abu al-'Aliya, Ikrimah, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Abu Nahik recited (tuhajirun) with a shadda on the jim and a damma on the ta. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is the same as the recitation of Ibn Abbas.

And "al-jinnah" means madness. ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾ He means: the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 71–73:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَلَوِ اتَّبَعَ الحَقُّ أهْواءَهُمْ﴾ في المُرادِ بِالحَقِّ قَوْلانِ:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾. Regarding what is meant by "the truth" there are two opinions:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ، وابْنُ جُرَيْجٍ، والسُّدِّيُّ في آخَرِينَ.

The first: it is Allah, mighty and majestic. This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, and others.

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ القُرْآنُ، ذَكَرَهُ الفَرّاءُ والزَّجّاجُ. فَعَلى القَوْلِ الأوَّلِ يَكُونُ المَعْنى: لَوْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لِنَفْسِهِ شَرِيكًا كَما يُحِبُّونَ. وعَلى الثّانِي: لَوْ نَزَلَ القُرْآنُ بِما يُحِبُّونَ مِن جَعْلِ شَرِيكٍ لِلَّهِ. ﴿لَفَسَدَتِ السَّماواتُ والأرْضُ ومَن فِيهِنَّ بَلْ أتَيْناهم بِذِكْرِهِمْ﴾؛ أيْ: بِما فِيهِ شَرَفُهم وفَخْرُهم، وهو القُرْآنُ. ﴿فَهم عَنْ ذِكْرِهِمْ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾؛ أيْ: قَدْ تَوَلَّوْا عَمّا جاءَهم مِن شَرَفِ الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ.

The second: it is the Qur'an, mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. According to the first opinion, the meaning is: if Allah had made a partner for Himself as they desire. According to the second: if the Qur'an had descended with what they desire of making a partner for Allah. ﴿The heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾; that is, that in which is their honour and pride, namely the Qur'an. ﴿But they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾; that is, they have turned away from what came to them of the honour of this world and the Hereafter.

وقَرَأ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ، وأُبَيُّ بْنُ كَعْبٍ، وأبُو رَجاءٍ، وأبُو الجَوْزاءِ: ( بَلْ أتَيْناهم بِذِكْراهم فَهم عَنْ ذِكْراهم مُعْرِضُونَ ) بِألِفٍ فِيهِما.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', and Abu al-Jawza' read: ( بَلْ أتَيْناهم بِذِكْراهم فَهم عَنْ ذِكْراهم مُعْرِضُونَ ) with an alif in both places.

﴿أمْ تَسْألُهُمْ﴾ عَمّا جِئْتَهم بِهِ، ﴿خَرْجًا﴾ (p-٤٨٥)قَرَأ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ، ونافِعٌ، وأبُو عَمْرٍو، وعاصِمٌ: ( خَرْجًا ) بِغَيْرِ ألِفٍ، [ ( فَخَراجُ ) بِألِفٍ ] . وقَرَأ ابْنُ عامِرٍ: ( خَرْجًا فَخَرْجُ ) بِغَيْرِ ألِفٍ في الحَرْفَيْنِ. وقَرَأ حَمْزَةُ والكِسائِيُّ: ( خَراجًا ) بِألِفٍ، ( فَخَراجُ ) بِألِفٍ في الحَرْفَيْنِ. ومَعْنى " خَرْجًا ": أجْرًا ومالًا.

﴿Or do you ask them for any payment﴾ for what you have brought them? ﴿khar'jan﴾ (p-٤٨٥). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read ( خَرْجًا ) without an alif, [ ( فَخَراجُ ) with an alif ]. Ibn 'Amir read ( خَرْجًا فَخَرْجُ ) without an alif in both words. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ( خَراجًا ) with an alif, and ( فَخَراجُ ) with an alif in both words. The meaning of "khar'jan" is wages and property.

﴿فَخَراجُ رَبِّكَ﴾؛ أيْ: فَما يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ مِن أجْرِهِ وثَوابِهِ، ﴿خَيْرٌ وهو خَيْرٌ الرّازِقِينَ﴾؛ أيْ: أفْضَلُ مَن أعْطى، وهَذا عَلى سَبِيلِ التَّنْبِيهِ لَهم أنَّهُ لَمْ يَسْألْهم أجْرًا، لا أنَّهُ قَدْ سَألَهم.

﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾; that is, what your Lord gives you of His reward and recompense, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾; that is, the most excellent of those who give. This is by way of alerting them that he did not ask them for any wage, not that he had in fact asked them.

والنّاكِبُ: العادِلُ، يُقالُ: نَكَبَ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ؛ أيْ: عَدَلَ عَنْهُ.

And "al-nakib" means one who deviates; it is said: "nakaba 'an al-tariq", meaning he deviated from the road.

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ القُرْآنُ، ذَكَرَهُ الفَرّاءُ والزَّجّاجُ. فَعَلى القَوْلِ الأوَّلِ يَكُونُ المَعْنى: لَوْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لِنَفْسِهِ شَرِيكًا كَما يُحِبُّونَ. وعَلى الثّانِي: لَوْ نَزَلَ القُرْآنُ بِما يُحِبُّونَ مِن جَعْلِ شَرِيكٍ لِلَّهِ. ﴿لَفَسَدَتِ السَّماواتُ والأرْضُ ومَن فِيهِنَّ بَلْ أتَيْناهم بِذِكْرِهِمْ﴾؛ أيْ: بِما فِيهِ شَرَفُهم وفَخْرُهم، وهو القُرْآنُ. ﴿فَهم عَنْ ذِكْرِهِمْ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾؛ أيْ: قَدْ تَوَلَّوْا عَمّا جاءَهم مِن شَرَفِ الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ.

The second: it is the Qur'an, mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. According to the first opinion, the meaning is: if Allah had made a partner for Himself as they desire. According to the second: if the Qur'an had descended with what they desire of making a partner for Allah. ﴿The heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾; that is, that in which is their honour and pride, namely the Qur'an. ﴿But they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾; that is, they have turned away from what came to them of the honour of this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', and Abu al-Jawza' read: ( بَلْ أتَيْناهم بِذِكْراهم فَهم عَنْ ذِكْراهم مُعْرِضُونَ ) with an alif in both places.

﴿أمْ تَسْألُهُمْ﴾ عَمّا جِئْتَهم بِهِ، ﴿خَرْجًا﴾ (p-٤٨٥)قَرَأ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ، ونافِعٌ، وأبُو عَمْرٍو، وعاصِمٌ: ( خَرْجًا ) بِغَيْرِ ألِفٍ، [ ( فَخَراجُ ) بِألِفٍ ] . وقَرَأ ابْنُ عامِرٍ: ( خَرْجًا فَخَرْجُ ) بِغَيْرِ ألِفٍ في الحَرْفَيْنِ. وقَرَأ حَمْزَةُ والكِسائِيُّ: ( خَراجًا ) بِألِفٍ، ( فَخَراجُ ) بِألِفٍ في الحَرْفَيْنِ. ومَعْنى " خَرْجًا ": أجْرًا ومالًا.

﴿Or do you ask them for any payment﴾ for what you have brought them? ﴿khar'jan﴾ (p-٤٨٥). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read ( خَرْجًا ) without an alif, [ ( فَخَراجُ ) with an alif ]. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 74–77:

Allah's words: ﴿And even if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicts them of adversity﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The adversity here is the famine (al-ju', hunger) that befell the people of Makkah when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against them, saying: 'O Allah, help me against Quraysh with years like the years of Yusuf.' Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and complained to him of the adversity, and that they had eaten the hide (qadd) and the bones. So this verse and the one after it were revealed, and the punishment mentioned in His words, ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾, is this."

Allah's words: ﴿Until when We open upon them a door of severe punishment﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: that it is the Day of Badr. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: that it is the hunger that afflicted them. This was said by Muqatil.

Third: that it is a door of the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter. This was related by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿Then they, in it, will be despairing﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Nahik, and Mu'adh al-Qari recited: "mublasun" (مُبْلَسُونَ) with a fatha on the lam. The meaning of mublis (مُبْلِس, one who is despairing, utterly hopeless) has already been explained in (al-An'am: 45).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verse 78–85:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks.﴾ The exegetes said: He means that they do not give thanks at all.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He multiplied you upon the earth.﴾ That is: He created you from the earth.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day.﴾ That is: He is the One who made them two alternating things, following each other and differing in darkness and light. ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ (i.e., will you not reflect on the workmanship you see?) As for what follows this, it is clear until His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?﴾ That is: say to the people of Makkah who deny the Resurrection: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it of creation, if you know its condition? ﴿They will say: "To Allah."﴾ Abu 'Amr recited: (lillahi) without an alif here, and in the two that follow it with an alif. The rest recited (lillahi) in all three places. Abu 'Amr's reading is in accordance with analogy (qiyas). Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever recites (sayaqulna Allahu) it is the direct answer to the question, and whoever recites (lillahi) it is also good, because when you say: "Who is the owner of this house?" and it is answered: "To Zayd," it is permissible, since the meaning of "Who is the owner of this house?" is "To whom does it belong?" Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Whoever recites (lillahi) in the other two places has answered according to the meaning rather than what the wording requires. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-Jawza' recited (sayaqulna Allahu), (Allahu), (Allahu) with an alif in all of them. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi said: It is in the codices of the people of Basra with an alif in all of them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Will you not then remember?﴾ So that you would know that He who is able to create that originally is more able to bring the dead back to life.

As for what follows this, it is clear until His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?﴾ That is: say to the people of Makkah who deny the Resurrection: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it of creation, if you know its condition? ﴿They will say: "To Allah."﴾ Abu 'Amr recited: (lillahi) without an alif here, and in the two that follow it with an alif. The rest recited (lillahi) in all three places. Abu 'Amr's reading is in accordance with analogy (qiyas). Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever recites (sayaqulna Allahu) it is the direct answer to the question, and whoever recites (lillahi) it is also good, because when you say: "Who is the owner of this house?" and it is answered: "To Zayd," it is permissible, since the meaning of "Who is the owner of this house?" is "To whom does it belong?" Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Whoever recites (lillahi) in the other two places has answered according to the meaning rather than what the wording requires. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-Jawza' recited (sayaqulna Allahu), (Allahu), (Allahu) with an alif in all of them. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi said: It is in the codices of the people of Basra with an alif in all of them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Will you not then remember?﴾ So that you would know that He who is able to create that originally is more able to bring the dead back to life.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 86–89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then fear (Allah)?﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: "Will you not then fear" means: will you not beware of worshipping other than Him. The second: will you not fear His punishment. As for the malakut (dominion, sovereignty), we have explained it in (al-An'am: 75).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Protector, and none can protect against Him﴾; that is: He prevents evil from whomever He wills, and no one can prevent from Him whoever He intends with evil. It is said: "ajartu fulanan," meaning: I protected him (ḥamaytuhu); and "ajartu 'alayhi," meaning: I protected against him (ḥamaytu 'anhu).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: How are you deceived and turned away from this?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 90–92:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth﴾; that is, with monotheism (tawhid) and the Qur'an. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ regarding what they attribute to God of offspring and partner. Then He negated both of them from Himself with what follows this, up to His saying: ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾; that is, he would have been singular in his creation, and would not have been pleased that his creation and his bounty be attributed to another, and he would have prevented the other god from seizing what he had created. ﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾; that is, some of them would have overpowered others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read (ʿĀlimi) with a kasra. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (ʿĀlimu) with a damma. Al-Akhfash said: the genitive (jarr) is better, so that the speech is of one aspect, and the nominative (raf') is on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and what strengthens it is that the first speech has ended.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 93–98:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If You should show me that which they are promised﴾. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and al-Dahhak read it as (tur'iʾnni), with a hamza between the ra' and the nun, without a ya'. The meaning is: If You show me what they are promised of killing and punishment, then make me outside of them and do not destroy me along with their destruction. So Allah, Exalted is He, showed him what He had promised them at Badr and other than it, and He saved him and those with him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

One: repel the wrong of the wrongdoer with forgiveness. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: repel obscenity with peace. This is the saying of 'Ata' and al-Dahhak.

The third: repel polytheism with monotheism. This is the saying of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fourth: repel wrongdoing with admonition. This is related by al-Mawardi. Some exegetes mentioned that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾; that is, of what they say of polytheism and denial, and the meaning is: We will requite them for that. ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge﴾; that is, I take refuge and keep away, ﴿in You from the whisperings of the devils﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is their pricking and their stinging. From this it is said of the fault-finder: a humazah (one who whispers slander), as if he stings and pricks when he finds fault. Ibn Faris said: al-hamz is like squeezing; it is said: "I squeezed the thing in my palm," and from it comes hamz in speech, because it is as if he presses the letter. Others said: al-hamz in the language means pushing, and the whisperings (hamazat) of the devils are their pushing of people through misguidance toward acts of disobedience.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That they should be present with me﴾; that is, that they should attend, and the meaning is: that they should harm me, because the devil does not attend a son of Adam except with harm. Then He informed that these disbelievers who deny the Resurrection ask for a return to the world at the time of death, by the verse that follows this one. It was also said: this request from them is directed to the angels who take their souls.

If it is asked: How did He say ﴿Return me﴾ when He means: Return me (singular)?

The answer: this form of expression is known to the Arabs for one of great rank, because He speaks of Himself with what a group speaks with, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We are the One who gives life and causes death﴾ [Qaf: 43], so His address comes like His report about Himself. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 99–104:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "In what has passed of my life." Muqatil said: "In what I have left behind of righteous deeds."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿No!﴾ That is, he will not be returned to the world. ﴿Indeed, it is a word he is saying﴾ meaning: his request for a return. ﴿It is only a word he is saying﴾ that is, it is speech with no benefit in it. ﴿And behind them﴾ that is, in front of them and before them, ﴿is a barrier (barzakh)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "The barzakh is what lies between this world and the Hereafter, and everything between two things is a barzakh." Al-Zajjaj said: "Barzakh linguistically means a barrier, and here it refers to what lies between the death of the deceased and his resurrection."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the Horn is blown﴾. Regarding this blowing there are two opinions:

The first: that it is the first blast. This was narrated by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that it is the second blast. This was narrated by ʿAtaʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So there will be no kinship among them﴾. In the statement there is an omitted element; its estimate is: there will be no kinship among them that day by which they boast or by which they sever ties, because kinship is not cut off that day; rather, mutual ties and boasting through them are removed.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And they will not ask of one another﴾ there are three opinions:

One of them: they will not ask one another by lineage that one should yield his right to another.

The second: none of them will ask another about his condition, because each is occupied with himself.

The third: none of them will ask another from which tribe he is, as the Arabs do, in order to know the lineage and thus know the standing of the man. What follows has already been explained [in Al-Aʿraf: 8] up to His saying: ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Talhah (scorches) and tanhah (blows upon) have the same meaning, except that laffh has a greater effect." Al-Kalih is the one whose lip has drawn back from his teeth, like what you see of the heads of sheep when the teeth are exposed and the lips are drawn up. Ibn Masʿud said: "Their teeth will be exposed and their lips will shrink back like a head roasted over fire." Abu ʿAbdullah al-Hakim narrated in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning this verse: "The Fire will disfigure him, so his upper lip will shrink until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip will hang down until it reaches his navel."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 23, verses 105–111:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ The meaning: it will be said to them, "Were not My verses recited to you," meaning the Qur'an. ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read shiqwatuna with a kasra on the shin and without an alif. 'Amr ibn al-'As, Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read it likewise, except with a fatha on the shin. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read shaqawatuna with an alif and a fatha on the shin and the qaf. It is also reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah likewise, except that the shin is kasra. The exegetes said: the people acknowledged that the wretchedness decreed upon them prevented them from guidance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it﴾; that is, from the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought to return to the world. ﴿And if we return﴾; that is, to disbelief and sins.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Be silent therein﴾. al-Zajjaj said: go away with the distance of wrath. It is said: "I drove away the dog (khasa'tu al-kalb, akhsa'uhu)" when you drive it off so that it goes away.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾; that is, regarding the lifting of the punishment from you. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: The people of Hell will call upon Malik for forty years, and he will not answer them. Then he will say: ﴿Indeed, you will remain [forever]﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 77]. Then they will call upon their Lord: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it﴾, and He will leave them for a length equal to the age of the world. Then He will say: ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾. Then they will call upon their Lord: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it﴾, and He will leave them for a length equal to the age of the world. Then He will reply to them: ﴿Be silent therein and do not speak to Me﴾. After that, the people will not utter a single word, except for the groaning and the sighing.

Then He explained the reason for which He silenced them, by His saying: "Indeed" (innahu). Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read it anna-hu with a fatha on the hamzah. ﴿There was a group of My servants﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the Emigrants (al-Muhajirin).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you took them﴾. al-Zajjaj said: The better reading is to assimilate the dhal into the ta', because the two makhraj (points of articulation) are close; and if you wish, you may pronounce them distinctly, because the dhal is from one word and the ta' is from another, and there is some distance between the dhal and the ta' in articulation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sikhriyyan (as a mockery)﴾. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Hatim from Ya'qub read sukhriyyan with a damma on the sin here and in (Sad: 63). al-Mufaddal agreed with them in (Sad: 32). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read it with a kasra on the sin in both surahs. There is no disagreement about the damma on the sin in the word in (az-Zukhruf: 32). al-Farra' preferred the damma, and al-Zajjaj preferred the kasra. Are the two of them the same in meaning? There are two views on this:

One: they are two dialects with one meaning, as said by al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and similar to the Arabs' saying: bahrun lujjiyyun and lijjiyyun, and kawkabun durriyyun and dirriyyun.

The second: the kasra means "mockery" (al-huzu), and the damma means "subjugation and enslavement" (al-sukhrah wa al-isti'bad). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, transmitted by al-Farra', and it is narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 23, verses 112–118:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He will say, "How long did you remain?"﴾ Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited (قالَ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ) *qala kam labithtum* ("He said, how long did you remain"). This is God's question to the disbelievers. There are two opinions about when it is asked:

One: He asks them on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: after they have entered the Fire.

Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited (قُلْ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ) *qul kam labithtum* ("Say, how long did you remain"). Regarding this reading there are two opinions:

One: It is addressed to each one of them, meaning: "Say, O disbeliever."

The second: the meaning is "Say (plural)," which is phrased in the form of a command to one person while the intended audience is a group, since the meaning is understood.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i assimilate the *tha'* of (لَبِثْتُمْ) *labithtum* into the following *ta'*, while the rest do not assimilate it. Whoever assimilates does so because the articulation points of *tha'* and *ta'* are close, and whoever does not assimilate does so because the two articulation points are distinct.

Regarding what is meant by "the earth," there are two opinions: One: that it means the graves. The second: that it means the world. The people belittled the length of their stay because of what they witnessed of the terrors and the punishment, so they said: ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is, "We do not know how long we remained."

Regarding what is meant by "those who count," there are two opinions:

One: the angels, as related by Mujahid.

The second: the reckoners (i.e., those who keep account), as related by Qatada. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Ya'mur recited (العادِينَ) *al-'adin* with the *dal* lightened (i.e., without the doubling).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He will say, "If you remained only a little, if only you had known."﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited (قالَ إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ) *qala in labithtum* ("He said, if you remained"). Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited (قُلْ إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ) *qul in labithtum* ("Say, if you remained"), meaning: "Say, O questioner about their stay." They claimed that in the *mushaf* (codex) of the people of Kufa the word (قُلْ) *qul* appears in both places, so Hamza and al-Kisa'i read them as they are written in their codices. The meaning is: you remained in the earth only a little, because their stay in the earth, however long, is finite, whereas their stay in the Fire has no end.

Regarding His saying, ﴿if you had only known﴾, there are two opinions:

One: if you had known the measure of your stay in the earth.

The second: if you had known that you would return to God, and had acted accordingly.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ meaning: did you suppose? ﴿Without purpose﴾ meaning: in vain. "Abath" (purposelessness) in the language means play, and it has been said it is an action performed without a sound purpose. ﴿And that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim recited (لا تُرْجَعُونَ) *la turja'un* with the *ta'* pronounced with a *damma* (i.e., "you will not be returned," in the passive). Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited it with a *fatha* (i.e., "you will not return," in the active).

﴿Exalted is God﴾ above what the ignorant ascribe to Him of association and offspring. ﴿The King﴾: al-Khattabi said: He is the one whose dominion is complete, encompassing all kinds of things that are owned. As for the *malik* (owner), he is the one whose ownership is exclusive. We have already mentioned the meaning of ﴿the Truth﴾ in (Surah Yunus, 32).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ "Noble" (karim), when applied to an inanimate thing, means "good." Ibn Muhaysin recited (الكَرِيمُ) *al-karimu* with a *damma* on the *mim* (i.e., as an attribute of God, "the Noble"), meaning God, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying: ﴿He has no proof for it﴾ meaning: he has no argument for it and no evidence. Some have said its meaning is: "so he has no proof for it."

His saying: ﴿His reckoning is only with his Lord﴾ meaning: his recompense is with his Lord.

Completed, by the help of God, Blessed and Exalted, is the fifth part of the book *Zad al-Masir fi 'Ilm al-Tafsir*, followed by the sixth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of *Surat al-Nur*.
